'''Bernd Fritzsch''' (born 1948)<ref name="fb1">{{cite book |last1=Fritzsch |first1=Bernd |last2=Elliott |first2=Karen L. |title=Catalogue record: Evolution of Neurosensory Cells and Systems (authority entry "Fritzsch, Bernd 1948–", GND 1132734150) |date=2022 |url=https://search.ub.tum.de/vufind/Record/DE-604.BV048463992 |publisher=Technical University of Munich Library |doi=10.1201/9781003092810 |isbn=978-1-003-09281-0 |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> is a [[Neuroscience|neurobiologist]] who studies how the vertebrate inner ear develops, how it evolved, and how it connects to the brainstem.<ref name="fb2">{{cite web |title=Bernd Fritzsch, PhD |url=https://www.unmc.edu/neurologicalsciences/about/faculty/fritzsch.html |publisher=Department of Neurological Sciences, University of Nebraska Medical Center |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="fb3">{{cite web |title=New faculty spotlight: Bernd Fritzsch, PhD |url=https://www.unmc.edu/newsroom/2023/09/12/new-faculty-spotlight-bernd-fritzsch-phd/ |publisher=University of Nebraska Medical Center |date=12 September 2023 |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="fb4">{{cite web |title=Professor Dr Bernd Fritzsch |url=https://www.leopoldina.org/en/members/list-of-members/list-of-members/member/Member/show/bernd-fritzsch/ |publisher=German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> He is a professor in the Department of Neurological Sciences at the [[University of Nebraska Medical Center]] (UNMC), which he joined in July 2023.<ref name="fb2" /><ref name="fb3" /> He previously held faculty positions at [[Creighton University]] and the [[University of Iowa]], where he chaired the Department of Biology from 2008 to 2016 and is professor emeritus.<ref name="fb4" /><ref name="fb5">{{cite web |title=Former iBio graduate students highlight the many accomplishments of Bernd Fritzsch, Biology's former departmental executive officer |url=https://biology.uiowa.edu/news/2020/10/former-ibio-graduate-students-highlight-many-accomplishments-bernd-fritzsch-biologys |publisher=Department of Biology, University of Iowa |date=27 October 2020 |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref>
 
His work in comparative molecular neuroembryology examines the genes that control the formation of hair cells, auditory and vestibular neurons, and their central targets, with the aim of identifying developmental steps relevant to restoring hearing.<ref name="fb4" /> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2009<ref name="fb6">{{cite journal |title=AAAS members elected as Fellows |journal=Science |volume=326 |issue=5960 |page=1656 |year=2009 |doi=10.1126/science.326.5960.1656}}</ref><ref name="fb7">{{cite web |title=Elected members & fellows |url=https://provost.uiowa.edu/elected-members-fellows |publisher=Office of the Provost, University of Iowa |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> and a member of the [[German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]] in 2015.<ref name="fb4" /><ref name="fb8">{{cite web |title=Nationalakademie Leopoldina ernennt neue Mitglieder |url=https://idw-online.de/de/news651366 |publisher=Leopoldina |via=Informationsdienst Wissenschaft |date=17 May 2016 |language=de |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref>
 
== Education ==
Fritzsch studied biology at the [[Technische Universität Darmstadt|Technical University of Darmstadt]] from 1968 to 1973 and completed his doctorate there in 1978, supported by a doctoral scholarship from the [[Studienstiftung des deutschen Volkes]] awarded in 1973.<ref name="fb4" /> His doctoral research examined how the ear connects to the brain in mice and chickens.<ref name="fb9">{{cite magazine |last=Keener |first=Amanda B. |date=September 2015 |title=Contributors |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/contributors-62-34909 |magazine=The Scientist |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> He completed his [[habilitation]] at [[Bielefeld University]] in 1985.<ref name="fb4" />
 
== Career ==
=== Germany and Scripps ===
Fritzsch was an assistant professor at TU Darmstadt from 1978 to 1981 and at Bielefeld University from 1981 to 1986.<ref name="fb4" /> In this period he worked on the [[lateral line]], [[electroreception]] and hearing in amphibians.<ref name="fb9" /> He held a Heisenberg Fellowship from the [[Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft|German Research Foundation]] (DFG) from 1986 to 1990,<ref name="fb4" /> and from 1988 to 1990 was a research fellow at the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]], University of California, San Diego, where he worked with R. Glenn Northcutt on the electroreceptive and mechanosensory systems of the [[axolotl]].<ref name="fb4" /><ref name="fb5" />
 
=== Creighton University ===
In 1991 he joined the Department of Biomedical Sciences at Creighton University in Omaha as an associate professor, becoming a full professor in 1993. He was Director of Basic Research from 2003 to 2008 and assistant dean for research at the medical school from 2004 to 2007.<ref name="fb3" /><ref name="fb4" /><ref name="fb5" /> His research has been supported by the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, NASA and the German Research Foundation.<ref name="fb5" /> In 2006 he and colleagues published a review of the molecular and developmental basis of the evolution of the vertebrate auditory system.<ref name="fb10">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |last2=Pauley |first2=S. |last3=Feng |first3=F. |last4=Matei |first4=V. |last5=Nichols |first5=D. H. |year=2006 |title=The molecular and developmental basis of the evolution of the vertebrate auditory system |journal=International Journal of Comparative Psychology |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=1–25 |doi=10.46867/ijcp.2006.19.01.06 |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0288b9qh}}</ref>
 
=== University of Iowa ===
Fritzsch moved to the University of Iowa in 2008 as professor and departmental executive officer (chair) of the Department of Biology, a post he held until 2016.<ref name="fb4" /><ref name="fb5" /> During his tenure as chair, the department added six faculty members and obtained a multidisciplinary NIH P30 centre grant, and the average time to complete a graduate degree fell from about seven to under five and a half years.<ref name="fb5" /> He was a co-investigator on that grant, the Iowa Center for Molecular Auditory Neuroscience (2010–2015).<ref name="fb11">{{cite web |title=Bernd Fritzsch |url=https://biology.uiowa.edu/people/bernd-fritzsch |publisher=Department of Biology, University of Iowa |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> He held the Endowed Iowa Entrepreneurial Professorship from 2008 to 2010.<ref name="fb4" />
 
He was co-director of the university's Aging Mind and Brain Initiative from 2011 to 2014 and its director from 2014 to 2019, and director of the University of Iowa Center on Aging from 2014 to 2018.<ref name="fb4" /> In 2014 he was named executive director of a pilot undergraduate science research programme in the Department of Biology, established with a US$1 million gift from Robert and Sue Latham.<ref name="fb12">{{cite web |last=Cummer |first=Jacob |date=29 September 2014 |title=Alumni couple gives $1 million to boost undergraduate research at the UI |url=https://now.uiowa.edu/news/2014/09/alumni-couple-gives-1-million-boost-undergraduate-research-ui |work=Iowa Now |publisher=University of Iowa |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> In 2016 he was named to the scientific advisory board of Decibel Therapeutics, a company developing treatments for hearing loss.<ref name="fb13">{{cite press release |title=Decibel Therapeutics assembles world-class scientific advisory board |url=https://www.biospace.com/decibel-therapeutics-assembles-world-class-scientific-advisory-board |publisher=Decibel Therapeutics |via=BioSpace |date=1 November 2016 |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref> He retired at the end of 2019 and became professor emeritus in 2020.<ref name="fb4" /><ref name="fb5" />
 
=== University of Nebraska Medical Center ===
In July 2023 Fritzsch joined UNMC as a professor in the Department of Neurological Sciences, where his laboratory studies ear and hair cell development, regeneration and evolution, as well as ear development in ageing.<ref name="fb2" /><ref name="fb3" /> This work is funded by the [[National Institute on Aging]] and the [[National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders]],<ref name="fb2" /> and since retiring from Iowa he has been a co-principal investigator on an NIH grant studying age-related hearing loss.<ref name="fb5" />
 
== Research ==
=== Lateral line and electroreception ===
In 1995 Northcutt, Kurt Brändle and Fritzsch removed and transplanted embryonic placodes in axolotls and found that many of the placodes that form mechanosensory lateral line organs also give rise to electroreceptive ampullary organs.<ref name="fb14">{{cite journal |last1=Northcutt |first1=R. G. |last2=Brändle |first2=K. |last3=Fritzsch |first3=B. |year=1995 |title=Electroreceptors and mechanosensory lateral line organs arise from single placodes in axolotls |journal=Developmental Biology |volume=168 |issue=2 |pages=358–373 |doi=10.1006/dbio.1995.1086 |pmid=7729575}}</ref>
 
=== Evolution of sensory systems ===
In 1987 Fritzsch reported a sensory structure in the inner ear of the [[coelacanth]] ''Latimeria'' that resembles the basilar papilla of tetrapods, and proposed that the two are homologous.<ref name="fb15">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |year=1987 |title=Inner ear of the coelacanth fish Latimeria has tetrapod affinities |journal=Nature |volume=327 |issue=6118 |pages=153–154 |doi=10.1038/327153a0 |pmid=22567677 |bibcode=1987Natur.327..153F }}</ref> A later anatomical study interpreted the coelacanth organ differently.<ref name="fb16">{{cite thesis |last=Bernstein |first=Peter |year=2001 |title=Die evolutive Transformation der Oticalregion der Sarcopterygii beim Übergang vom Wasser- zum Landleben |type=Doctoral thesis |publisher=University of Tübingen |url=https://publikationen.uni-tuebingen.de/xmlui/handle/10900/48320 |language=de}}</ref> He was a co-author of a 2026 study proposing that extinct coelacanths used an ossified lung to transmit sound to the inner ear.<ref name="fb17">{{cite journal |last1=Manuelli |first1=L. |last2=Clément |first2=G. |last3=Herbin |first3=M. |last4=Fritzsch |first4=B. |last5=Ahlberg |first5=P. E. |last6=Dollman |first6=K. |last7=Cavin |first7=L. |year=2026 |title=A dual respiratory and auditory function for the coelacanth lung |journal=Communications Biology |volume=9 |issue=1 |article-number=400 |doi=10.1038/s42003-026-09708-6 |doi-access=free |pmid=41691076 |pmc=13003144 }}</ref> He was also a contributor to the 2013 sequencing of the [[sea lamprey]] genome.<ref name="fb18">{{cite journal |last1=Smith |first1=J. J. |last2=Kuraku |first2=S. |last3=Holt |first3=C. |year=2013 |title=Sequencing of the sea lamprey (Petromyzon marinus) genome provides insights into vertebrate evolution |journal=Nature Genetics |display-authors=etal |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=415–421 |doi=10.1038/ng.2568 |pmid=23435085 |pmc=3709584 }}</ref> He has written correspondence in ''Science'' on the shared evolutionary origins of light and mechanical sensing (2005) and on electric organs (2014).<ref name="fb19">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |last2=Piatigorsky |first2=J. |year=2005 |title=Ancestry of photic and mechanic sensation? |journal=Science |volume=308 |issue=5725 |pages=1113–1114 |doi=10.1126/science.308.5725.1113 |pmid=15908343 }}</ref><ref name="fb20">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |year=2014 |title=Electric organs: history and potential |journal=Science |volume=345 |issue=6197 |pages=631–632 |doi=10.1126/science.345.6197.631-b |pmid=25104375}}</ref>
 
=== Eye muscle innervation ===
Fritzsch's early research addressed the development and evolution of eye muscle innervation.<ref name="fb4" /> Working with [[Sten Grillner]]'s group, he mapped the motor nuclei supplying the six eye muscles of the lamprey and found that, unlike in jawed vertebrates, the [[oculomotor nerve]] supplies only three of them (1990).<ref name="fb21">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |last2=Sonntag |first2=R. |last3=Dubuc |first3=R. |last4=Ohta |first4=Y. |last5=Grillner |first5=S. |year=1990 |title=Organization of the six motor nuclei innervating the ocular muscles in lamprey |journal=Journal of Comparative Neurology |volume=294 |issue=4 |pages=491–506 |doi=10.1002/cne.902940402 |pmid=2341623}}</ref> In 1995, with Andrew McMahon's group, he reported that oculomotor and trochlear nerves and motoneurons could not be labelled in mice lacking [[WNT1|Wnt1]], concluding that without Wnt1 these neurons either fail to form or do not survive.<ref name="fb22">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |last2=Nichols |first2=D. H. |last3=Echelard |first3=Y. |last4=McMahon |first4=A. P. |year=1995 |title=Development of midbrain and anterior hindbrain ocular motoneurons in normal and Wnt-1 knockout mice |journal=Journal of Neurobiology |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=457–469 |doi=10.1002/neu.480270403 |pmid=7561827}}</ref> A 1997 study he co-authored with McMahon's group provided evidence that [[Fibroblast growth factor 8|FGF8]] signalling from the boundary between midbrain and hindbrain controls the growth and patterning of the developing midbrain.<ref name="fb23">{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=S. M. K. |last2=Danielian |first2=P. S. |last3=Fritzsch |first3=B. |last4=McMahon |first4=A. P. |year=1997 |title=Evidence that FGF8 signalling from the midbrain-hindbrain junction regulates growth and polarity in the developing midbrain |journal=Development |volume=124 |issue=5 |pages=959–969 |doi=10.1242/dev.124.5.959 |doi-access=free |pmid=9056772}}</ref> In 2014 he was a co-author, with Elizabeth Engle's group, of a study showing that mice carrying the mouse equivalent of the most common human mutation in the kinesin [[KIF21A]] develop [[congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles]], with stalling of developing oculomotor axons.<ref name="fb24">{{cite web |title=Researchers track down cause of eye mobility disorder |url=https://now.uiowa.edu/node/33201 |work=Iowa Now |publisher=University of Iowa |date=16 April 2014 |access-date=29 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="fb25">{{cite journal |last1=Cheng |first1=L. |last2=Desai |first2=J. |last3=Miranda |first3=C. J. |year=2014 |title=Human CFEOM1 mutations attenuate KIF21A autoinhibition and cause oculomotor axon stalling |journal=Neuron |display-authors=etal |volume=82 |issue=2 |pages=334–349 |doi=10.1016/j.neuron.2014.02.038 |pmid=24656932 |pmc=4002761 }}</ref>
 
=== Inner ear development and hearing ===
Fritzsch's work on neurotrophins showed that mice lacking [[neurotrophin-3]] lose all sensory neurons in the basal turn of the [[cochlea]] and many in the middle and apical turns (1997),<ref name="fb26">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |last2=Fariñas |first2=I. |last3=Reichardt |first3=L. F. |year=1997 |title=Lack of neurotrophin 3 causes losses of both classes of spiral ganglion neurons in the cochlea in a region-specific fashion |journal=Journal of Neuroscience |volume=17 |issue=16 |pages=6213–6225 |doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.17-16-06213.1997 |pmid=9236232 |pmc=2693053 }}</ref> and a 1997 review he led summarised how BDNF, NT-3 and their receptors support inner ear innervation.<ref name="fb27">{{cite journal |last1=Fritzsch |first1=B. |last2=Silos-Santiago |first2=I. |last3=Bianchi |first3=L. M. |last4=Fariñas |first4=I. |year=1997 |title=The role of neurotrophic factors in regulating the development of inner ear innervation |journal=Trends in Neurosciences |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=159–164 |doi=10.1016/S0166-2236(96)01007-7 |pmid=9106356}}</ref> He has studied the transcription factors that produce [[hair cell]]s and auditory neurons, showing that ears of Neurogenin 1 null mice form fewer hair cells and lack innervation (2000)<ref name="fb28">{{cite journal |last1=Ma |first1=Q. |last2=Anderson |first2=D. J. |last3=Fritzsch |first3=B. |year=2000 |title=Neurogenin 1 null mutant ears develop fewer, morphologically normal hair cells in smaller sensory epithelia devoid of innervation |journal=Journal of the Association for Research in Otolaryngology |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=129–143 |doi=10.1007/s101620010017 |pmid=11545141 |pmc=2504536 }}</ref> and that NeuroD null mice are deaf because of a severe loss of inner ear sensory neurons (2001).<ref name="fb29">{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=W. Y. |last2=Fritzsch |first2=B. |last3=Serls |first3=A. |year=2001 |title=NeuroD-null mice are deaf due to a severe loss of the inner ear sensory neurons during development |journal=Development |display-authors=etal |volume=128 |issue=3 |pages=417–426 |doi=10.1242/dev.128.3.417 |doi-access=free |pmid=11152640 |pmc=2710102 }}</ref> In 2022 he and colleagues reported that mice lacking the transcription factor ISL1 in their auditory neurons had impaired hearing and a disrupted frequency (tonotopic) map in the auditory pathway.<ref name="fb30">{{cite journal |last1=Filova |first1=I. |last2=Pysanenko |first2=K. |last3=Tavakoli |first3=M. |year=2022 |title=ISL1 is necessary for auditory neuron development and contributes toward tonotopic organization |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |display-authors=etal |volume=119 |issue=37 |article-number=e2207433119 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2207433119 |doi-access=free |pmid=36074819 |pmc=9478650 |bibcode=2022PNAS..11907433F }}</ref> He co-authored reviews of auditory system development in the ''Annual Review of Neuroscience'' in 2002 and 2024.<ref name="fb31">{{cite journal |last1=Rubel |first1=E. W. |last2=Fritzsch |first2=B. |year=2002 |title=Auditory system development: primary auditory neurons and their targets |journal=Annual Review of Neuroscience |volume=25 |pages=51–101 |doi=10.1146/annurev.neuro.25.112701.142849 |pmid=12052904}}</ref><ref name="fb32">{{cite journal |last1=Pyott |first1=S. J. |last2=Pavlinkova |first2=G. |last3=Yamoah |first3=E. N. |last4=Fritzsch |first4=B. |year=2024 |title=Harmony in the molecular orchestra of hearing: developmental mechanisms from the ear to the brain |journal=Annual Review of Neuroscience |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1146/annurev-neuro-081423-093942 |pmid=38360566 |pmc=11787624 }}</ref>
 
=== Vestibular development in spaceflight ===
Fritzsch contributed to a study of rats flown on NASA's [[Space Shuttle]] during pregnancy, which found that prenatal spaceflight altered vestibular behaviour and the branching of gravity-sensing afferents in the offspring (2008).<ref name="fb33">{{cite journal |last1=Ronca |first1=A. E. |last2=Fritzsch |first2=B. |last3=Bruce |first3=L. L. |last4=Alberts |first4=J. R. |year=2008 |title=Orbital spaceflight during pregnancy shapes function of mammalian vestibular system |journal=Behavioral Neuroscience |volume=122 |issue=1 |pages=224–232 |doi=10.1037/0735-7044.122.1.224 |pmid=18298265 |pmc=2610337 }}</ref>
